## Observations

1. In a concatenation, each value \(x\) contributes \(x\) multiplied by \(10\) to the power of the total number of digits after it.
2. If the set of values after \(x\) is a fixed \(k\)-element subset of the other values, exactly \(k!(N-1-k)!\) permutations realize that set.
3. Writing \(w_x=10^{\operatorname{digits}(x)}\), the coefficient of \(t^k\) in \(Q(t)/(1+w_xt)\), where \(Q(t)=\prod_{y=1}^{N}(1+w_yt)\), sums the shift multipliers for all \(k\)-element sets after \(x\). Values with the same digit length share this polynomial.
4. There are at most six distinct weights. Grouping equal factors in \(Q\) makes its logarithmic derivative a sum with at most six terms, giving a short recurrence for the coefficients of \(Q\).
5. Only coefficients of degrees \(0\) through \(N-1\) are needed, and every positive integer up to \(N\) is invertible modulo \(998244353\).

## Solution sketch

> In a concatenation, each value \(x\) contributes \(x\) multiplied by \(10\) to the power of the total number of digits after it.

1. Split \(1,\ldots,N\) into nonempty digit-length groups. For each group \(d\), record its count \(c_d\), its sum of values \(s_d\), and its weight \(w_d=10^d\). These can be obtained from the endpoints of each digit range, clipped at \(N\). A value in the suffix contributes one factor of its group's weight to the shift multiplier.

> If the set of values after \(x\) is a fixed \(k\)-element subset of the other values, exactly \(k!(N-1-k)!\) permutations realize that set.

2. Precompute factorials through \(N-1\) modulo \(998244353\). For a suffix set of size \(k\), the \(k\) suffix values can be ordered independently of the \(N-1-k\) prefix values, so its shift multiplier must be counted \(k!(N-1-k)!\) times.

> There are at most six distinct weights. Grouping equal factors in \(Q\) makes its logarithmic derivative a sum with at most six terms, giving a short recurrence for the coefficients of \(Q\).

3. Form the small polynomials
   \[
   R(t)=\prod_d(1+w_dt),\qquad
   H(t)=\sum_d c_dw_d\,\frac{R(t)}{1+w_dt}.
   \]
   Differentiating the grouped product \(Q(t)=\prod_d(1+w_dt)^{c_d}\) gives \(R(t)Q'(t)=H(t)Q(t)\). Start with \(q_0=1\), where \(q_m=[t^m]Q(t)\). For each \(m=1,\ldots,N-1\), compare coefficients of \(t^{m-1}\) in the identity. Since \(R(0)=1\), the only term involving \(q_m\) is \(m q_m\) on the left. Move the other left-hand terms to the right and multiply by the modular inverse of \(m\). Each coefficient takes work proportional to the number of groups.

> Writing \(w_x=10^{\operatorname{digits}(x)}\), the coefficient of \(t^k\) in \(Q(t)/(1+w_xt)\), where \(Q(t)=\prod_{y=1}^{N}(1+w_yt)\), sums the shift multipliers for all \(k\)-element sets after \(x\). Values with the same digit length share this polynomial.

4. For each group \(d\), generate the quotient coefficients in order: start with \(b_0=1\), then use \(b_k=q_k-w_db_{k-1}\). This follows by multiplying the quotient by \(1+w_dt\) and matching coefficients. Add
   \[
   s_d\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} b_k\,k!(N-1-k)!
   \]
   to the answer. The factorials count the permutations for each suffix set, and \(s_d\) accounts for all possible values \(x\) in the group. Print the accumulated answer modulo \(998244353\).

> Only coefficients of degrees \(0\) through \(N-1\) are needed, and every positive integer up to \(N\) is invertible modulo \(998244353\).

5. Perform all coefficient arithmetic modulo \(998244353\), precomputing the required inverses in linear time with the standard prime-modulus inverse recurrence. For \(N=1\), no inverse or positive-degree coefficient is needed: the single term uses \(b_0=1\) and \(0!=1\), yielding \(1\). With \(D\le 6\) nonempty groups, building \(R\) and \(H\) takes \(O(D^2)\) time using multiplication and exact division by linear factors. The coefficient passes take \(O(DN)\) time, and total space is \(O(N+D)\) because each quotient needs only its previous coefficient.
